## 7 Limitations

The measurements cover seven parameterized task families and three model profiles.
The online simulations use given family labels, fixed cost profiles, and reported failure causes.
Their savings depend on how costs and compilation outcomes are assigned to arriving task families.
Historical mean costs do not provide the action bounds required for the cost guarantee.
The live study tests fallback and call reservations for a fixed program, without evaluating the full online compilation algorithm.
Silent program failures and recovery from partially changed interfaces require further evaluation.
We measure model-token cost and exclude latency, device use, and program-maintenance effort.
Model and provider updates can change the measured costs.

## 8 Conclusion

PACE measures successful and failed compilation costs and per-use savings, then uses these profiles to make cost-aware compilation proposals.
Execution and compilation checks use the budget from observed arrivals to enforce K_{t}\leq(1+\epsilon)A_{t} under valid action-cost bounds.
For successful compilation attempts, estimated payback counts excluding source agent runs are 2 – 16 uses.
In simulations using recorded task arrivals, PACE saves 17.3\% relative to ReAct, 24.9\% relative to the AutoRPA adaptation, and 17.3\% relative to the ToolPro adaptation ( \epsilon=0.25 ).
Ablations separate the effects of the savings test, failed-attempt cost, and the cost budget.

### AI use statement

We used AI tools for finding relevant literature, drafting and revising text, and implementing the measurement and evaluation methods.
The tools also helped plan experiments, combine and interpret recorded results, develop and check mathematical arguments, and prepare tables and figures.
AI-generated programs are also part of the compilation method evaluated in Section 3.
We have reviewed all AI-assisted work.
We take responsibility for the final content of this paper.

### Ethics statement

The study uses benchmark applications, an Android emulator, desktop applications in a Linux container, and locally hosted web applications.
The arrival experiments use public event logs.
The study does not involve recruiting human participants or executing generated actions on users’ personal accounts.
Our cost bound does not ensure task correctness, so applying the method to actions with important real-world effects would require checks appropriate to those actions.

### Reproducibility statement

The code and saved records are at https://github.com/myl7/computer-use.
Appendix A describes the task families, recorded model identifiers, cost calculations, and verification procedures.
Section 4.3 states and proves the cost bound, and Appendix B gives the complete execution order and reference calculations.
Appendix C specifies the experimental grids, arrival logs, estimates of missing costs, paired outcomes, and confidence interval calculation.
